priority: Your work is document-primary. The monitor is the most important purchase.

2D drafting responds most to single-core CPU performance but most options will be good. If you have heavy XREF, block, and nested file usage, RAM and storage speed can play into the equation. In general, the quality of the monitor matters more than the computer to get great output.

BIM modeling is single-thread CPU bound. Clock speed for comparable processor generations governs how Revit, Rhino, and SketchUp feel, and AMD's X3D chips give a measurable responsiveness edge in Revit. The GPU doesn't affect viewport performance much.

Interactive rendering is driven almost entirely by the GPU choice. Enscape, Lumion, D5, and TwinMotion scale directly with GPU power and VRAM. The RTX 5070 Ti hits the practical sweet spot for most architecture viz but the sky is the limit and more GPU power means faster rendering and more complex scenes are supported.
You need both a CPU with fast single-core performance for modeling and a capable GPU for visualization.

V-Ray CPU and Corona are multi-thread CPU bound, with GPU hybrid modes available. Core count drives render times - AMD Ryzen 9 leads, and Threadripper PRO pulls further ahead if you're only rendering on that computer. GPU rendering continues to advance and it may be worth investigating switching away from CPU rendering.

2D drafting on Mac is well-served by the M4 Pro.
ArchiCAD, Vectorworks, SketchUp, Rhino v8 all run on Mac. Performance scales with GPU cores and unified memory.
Enscape works on Mac. TwinMotion runs via Rosetta. Lumion and D5 are Windows-only.
Unified memory serves as both RAM and VRAM.
V-Ray supports Metal GPU since V-Ray 7. A mid-range Windows PC with an RTX 4070 still outrenders a maxed Mac Studio. Mac wins on ecosystem, display, and silence.
